title: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Flightlessness of birds on predator-free oceanic islands is caused by disuse

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The nearly wingless condition of several birds living on oceanic islands that lack beasts of prey has been caused by disuse of the wings.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I believe that the nearly wingless condition of several birds, which now inhabit or have lately inhabited several oceanic islands, tenanted by no beast of prey, has been caused by disuse.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Use and disuse, combined with natural selection; organs of flight and of vision.”. Scope: birds of oceanic islands

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-03: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.61

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing phylogenomic and anatomical data can evaluate competing explanations for many island birds. The specific inheritance of acquired disuse is difficult to operationalize historically and cannot be directly observed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reconstruct independent island bird transitions to flightlessness and compare timing with predator absence, while examining genomic and anatomical signatures of relaxed selection versus adaptive energetic or survival selection. Evidence uniquely consistent with inherited effects of reduced wing use would support disuse; adaptive loss or drift would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Predator absence covaries with island ecology and energetic selection.

Darwinian 'disuse' does not map uniquely to a modern genetic mechanism.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The association between reduced flight and predator-poor islands is operational and the bird datasets cover that scope well enough for a standard comparative test. The causal wording attributes the condition to disuse, which those datasets do not measure and which selection explains equally well. The resolvable part is the pattern; the mechanism remains confounded.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Regress hand-wing index, or a flightless classification, on oceanic-island isolation and the absence of mammalian predators, with phylogeny controlled. Concentration of flightlessness on predator-free islands would confirm the geographic pattern. It would not confirm disuse, because selection against the cost of flight predicts the same distribution; a disuse-specific test would require a heritable effect of not flying that is independent of survival differences.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Disuse and selection against flight are not separated by wing measurements and island lists.

AVONET covers living birds and under-represents recently extinct island forms.

Predator-free is inferred from island faunas rather than measured predation rates.
